t: #2585 Number of Ways to Earn Points
o: This is a bounded knapsack: choose how many questions of each type to answer (at most countᵢ) so the marks sum to exactly target, counting combinations modulo 1e9+7. With target ≤ 1000, ≤50 types and counts/marks ≤ 50, even the naive triple loop (≈ 1000 · Σcountᵢ ≤ 2.5M states-transitions) is fast. Example 1 decomposes 6 points in 7 ways across the three types.
k: Process types one at a time; dp[j] = ways to reach exactly j points using processed types.
For each type, trying every count c from 0..countᵢ gives the bounded-knapsack transition.
Questions of the same type are indistinguishable, so choosing c of them is one decision, not C(count,c) combinations.

a.i: Keep dp over achievable point totals. For each type, build a fresh layer ndp where ndp[j] = Σ over valid c of dp[j − c·marks]; replacing dp wholesale per type prevents reusing the same type twice within one layer.
s: For each (count, marks): ndp[j] = Σ_{c=0..count, c·marks ≤ j} dp[j − c·marks].
a.t: O(target · Σ countᵢ) ≈ 2.5M transitions worst case

a.i: Define go(i, rem) = number of ways to make rem points using types i..n−1, branching on how many questions of type i to solve. Memoization on (i, rem) visits at most n·target states with the same transition sum.
s: go(i, rem): if i == n return rem == 0.
Otherwise sum go(i+1, rem − c·marks) for c = 0..countᵢ with c·marks ≤ rem.
a.t: O(n · target · maxCount) states-transitions, same asymptotics as Approach 1
a.sp: O(n · target) for the memo table

w: Use the iterative 1-D knapsack in an interview — it avoids recursion-depth concerns. Common pitfall: treating questions of a type as distinguishable (which would multiply by binomials) or reusing a type multiple times by doing the transition in place forward. Follow-up: with huge counts you would optimize the inner loop with prefix sums or the sliding-window trick for bounded knapsacks.
